title: Cat Pee Contains a Hidden Chemical 'ID Card,' Scientists Find
summary:
Cats live in a world of smell. They leave urine marks that carry messages long after they walk away. But most odor molecules evaporate or break down quickly — so how can another cat still tell who was there?

A team from Japan, Germany, and Spain, led by Iwate University, may have found the answer: 13 branched-chain fatty acids, or BFAs, that act like a durable chemical calling card. The study will appear in Current Biology.

First, the researchers confirmed that cats really can tell individual urine scents apart. When cats encountered the same sample repeatedly, they sniffed it less each time. But a different cat's urine sparked fresh interest. Remarkably, cats still showed reduced responses to old scents after gaps of months — suggesting long-term memory for urine odors.

The team also tracked the flehmen response, that open-mouthed, puzzled look cats make when investigating certain smells. Cats did it more often for unfamiliar urine than their own, and the response faded with repeated exposure — then jumped again when a new cat's sample appeared.

Guided by that behavior, scientists isolated the BFA fraction. Each cat had a unique profile — a specific combination and abundance of the 13 compounds — that stayed stable across different sampling dates. Related cats had more similar patterns, hinting that genetics plays a role, though each animal kept its own signature.

Crucially, BFAs are semi-volatile, meaning they evaporate slowly. In urine-soaked samples stored at 25°C, individual profiles remained stable for at least 24 hours.

So next time your cat sniffs a spot and makes that weird face, remember: it may be reading a message left hours — or months — ago.
why_it_matters: Understanding how cats identify each other by smell has practical consequences: it can shape how shelters, vets and people manage colonies of stray cats, and it explains why urine marking is communication rather than just bad behaviour. More broadly, it shows how long-lived chemical signals structure the social lives of animals humans live alongside — and it suggests that scent, not sight or sound, may carry much of the information in those relationships.

background_read: Cats are highly territorial: they rub their cheeks on furniture, scratch trees and spray urine to leave messages for other cats without having to fight, and a cat's nose has many more smell receptors than a human's.

When a cat sniffs something strange and then freezes with its mouth slightly open, that is the flehmen response, also called the Flehmen reaction — the pose helps scent reach a special sense organ, the vomeronasal organ, on the roof of its mouth, which detects chemical signals.
Current Biology (a journal published by Cell Press that covers every area of biology) will carry the study, which was led by Iwate University in Japan with researchers from Germany and Spain.

Fatty acids are basic building blocks of fats and oils, and the branched-chain type found here has an unusual shape — which may be exactly why it lingers in the air long enough to be read as an 'ID card'.
Scent-based identity is common among mammals, from mice to lions, so this discovery fits a much broader pattern of chemical communication that keeps working long after the animal has walked away.

perspectives.description: For cat owners, vets and shelters, this is genuinely useful knowledge: if cats leave and read long-lasting 'ID cards', then urine marking is a message, not simply a mess to punish. Understanding that could reduce stress for indoor cats and lead to better ways of managing multi-cat homes and rescue colonies.

The study focuses on a defined set of 13 compounds, and it is possible other signals are involved that were not measured. There is also a welfare angle: experiments that present cats with urine samples and watch their responses need careful ethical oversight, and results from laboratory settings may not reflect how cats behave outdoors.

Chemical identity signals are widespread among mammals, so this finding fits an established pattern rather than standing alone — what is new is pinning down which molecules carry the message and how slowly they fade. It also highlights how much animal communication happens on channels humans cannot detect at all.

The next questions are which genes build each cat's BFA profile, and whether close wild relatives such as lions and tigers use the same system. If the chemistry holds up, scent profiles could become a non-invasive way to identify individual wild cats from the marks they leave behind, without ever trapping or handling them.
